# The Value of Disagreement: Why the Best Meetings Don't End in Consensus

## Rethinking What a Successful Meeting Looks Like

There is a common assumption, woven deep into workplace culture, that a good meeting is one where everyone leaves nodding. The room reaches agreement, heads bob, someone volunteers to "circle back," and everyone walks out feeling productive. But this picture of success deserves scrutiny. Agreement, it turns out, can be deceptive. It can paper over genuine uncertainty, mask unspoken doubts, and create the illusion of alignment where none actually exists.

A truly productive meeting might look quite different. Rather than ending with everyone agreeing, it could end with something more valuable: a precise, honest description of what people actually disagree about, what evidence would settle the question, and who has committed to gathering that evidence. This is a harder standard than consensus, but it is a more honest and ultimately more useful one.

## The Trouble with Agreement

Why is agreement so often hollow? Consider a familiar scenario. A product team meets to decide whether to launch a new feature.
